g.text: The same datum has three different sets of requirements, depending on how old it is
One engine for a 1 GB expiring cache, a 1.15 TB/day append stream and a social graph would be wrong for at least two of them.
live location
location history
users & friendships
lifetime
600 SECONDS
permanent
permanent
volume
~1 GB total
1.15 TB / DAY
~100 GB (200 GB stored)
write rate
333k/sec
333k/sec
negligible
read rate
bulk read on connect only
almost never (analytics)
once per connect
durability
NONE NEEDED
required
required
on the hot path?
write yes, read no
no
no
engine
Redis (KV + TTL)
Cassandra (LSM), via Kafka
sharded relational
The split is not premature optimization - the requirements genuinely diverge on EVERY row.
live location - Redis
KEY loc:{user_id}
VALUE packed (lat f32, lng f32, ts u32) # 12 bytes
TTL 600 s, reset on every write
the TTL is doing three jobs at once
memory bound
10M x ~100 B ~= 1 GB - and it CANNOT grow,
regardless of how many of the 1B registered
users exist.
staleness bound
no position older than 10 minutes can ever
be read, so a stale value cannot be served
as current.
presence
key present = active, key gone = invisible.
No heartbeats, no presence service, no
online/offline events to order and reconcile.
Why a cache and not a database: the data is worthless in 30
seconds and self-correcting - the next update overwrites it
regardless of what happened to the last. There is nothing
for durability to protect. Paying for replication, WAL
writes and failover on data with a 30-second half-life
would be spending the wallet's budget on a weather forecast.
And float32 is FINE here, unlike prices or money. ~7
significant digits puts latitude within ~1 metre - far below
consumer GPS accuracy (3-10 m open, much worse in cities).
The MEASUREMENT error dwarfs the representation error, so
the precision loss is unobservable. Money has no measurement
error, so representation error is the only error there is -
which is why 'never use floats' is a rule about money, not
about numbers.
No spatial index: positions are looked up by user_id, never by
proximity. Sharded on user_id by consistent hashing, so the
init MGET fans out across shards in parallel.
location history - Cassandra
CREATE TABLE location_history (
user_id bigint,
bucket int, -- DAY NUMBER: bounds the partition
ts timestamp,
lat float,
lng float,
accuracy_m smallint,
PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, bucket), ts)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (ts DESC)
AND compaction = {'class': 'TimeWindowCompaction...'};
Why Cassandra, not the relational store: 333,000 appends/sec
with essentially no reads - the most write-skewed profile in
the design. LSM storage turns every write into a sequential
memtable append plus an eventual SSTable flush: no in-place
page updates, no B-tree splits. A relational store at this
rate would spend its life on random writes and index
maintenance for data nobody queries interactively.
Why the partition key is (user_id, bucket) and not just
user_id: one active user contributes ~2,880 rows/day, so a
year is a million-row partition and several years no longer
fits comfortably on one node. A Cassandra partition is the
unit of storage AND of repair, so unbounded growth is a real
operational problem. A day bucket bounds every partition BY
CONSTRUCTION; the cost is that a multi-day query reads
several partitions - fine, since history has no latency
requirement.
ts DESC because history queries are 'recent first': the
newest rows are physically first, so a LIMIT query stops
immediately instead of reverse-scanning the partition.
TimeWindowCompactionStrategy groups SSTables by time window,
so expiring old data DROPS WHOLE FILES rather than rewriting
them - the same principle as the message queue's segments.
Kafka sits in front, partitioned by user_id, for two reasons:
it decouples the WS server's latency from Cassandra's, so a
Cassandra hiccup cannot touch the live path; and it is a
replay buffer, so an outage causes a DELAY rather than a
permanent gap.
users & friendships - sharded relational
users
PK user_id
BIGINT
display_name
VARCHAR(64)
sharing_enabled
BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE
radius_m
INT DEFAULT 8047
created_at
TIMESTAMP
friendships
PK user_id
BIGINT
PK friend_id
BIGINT
created_at
TIMESTAMP
stored BIDIRECTIONALLY: (A,B) and
(B,A) are both inserted
Why both directions. The one query this table exists to serve
is friendsOf(user_id), run once per connection. One row per
pair would make it WHERE user_id = ? OR friend_id = ? - which
cannot use a single index efficiently and, once sharded on
user_id, becomes a SCATTER-GATHER ACROSS EVERY SHARD to find
rows where the user appears in the second column.
Duplicating the row makes friendsOf a single-shard,
single-index range scan, with PRIMARY KEY (user_id, friend_id)
clustering all of one user's friends together. The cost is 2x
storage and the obligation to write both rows in one
transaction. Trading storage for the elimination of a
scatter-gather on the connect path is straightforwardly
correct.
sharing_enabled DEFAULT FALSE puts the opt-in in the SCHEMA
rather than in application code: a bug in a settings screen
must not be able to turn on location sharing for someone who
never asked. Defaults are the cheapest place to encode a
privacy requirement.
This store must be sized for the RECONNECT STORM, not for
steady state: read rate is driven by connection churn, so
steady state is near-zero and a mass reconnect is briefly 10M
reads. An unusual sizing criterion, driven by a failure mode.
Deliberately absent
no geospatial index on live positions an index updated 333,000 times a second costs more than 40 pairwise haversines
no index on ts in the live cache freshness is enforced by the TTL, not by a query
no secondary index on location_history a Cassandra secondary index on a high-cardinality column is a known anti-pattern;
analytics queries go to the warehouse copy, not to Cassandra
no friend_count on users tempting for whale detection, but it would need maintaining on every friendship
change to answer an operational question a periodic batch job answers just as well
Where the guarantees go - and note that they run OPPOSITE to volume
live location EVENTUAL, last-write-wins, bounded by TTL each key has exactly ONE writer - the server holding
that connection - so there is no write conflict to
resolve. A 30-second-stale read is the product, not a
compromise.
location fan-out AT-MOST-ONCE, unordered ordering is resolved at the RECEIVER by timestamp;
an ordered transport would cost far more than it is worth
location history EVENTUAL, at-least-once a duplicate row with the same (user_id, bucket, ts) key
is an idempotent overwrite in Cassandra - duplication is
harmless BY CONSTRUCTION, so exactly-once is wasted effort
friendships STRONG, read-your-writes a new friend not immediately visible never gets
subscribed, and silently does not appear
sharing_enabled / radius STRONG turning sharing OFF must take effect immediately and must
never be read from a lagging replica - the failure mode is
leaking a location the user just asked to stop sharing
The asymmetry worth naming: the WEAKEST guarantees apply to the highest-volume data (positions, 333k/sec) and the STRONGEST
to the lowest-volume data (privacy settings, a handful per second). That is the correct arrangement, and it is the inverse of
what a uniform 'we use a strongly consistent database' approach produces - which spends the strong-consistency budget on the
data that needs it least.
What you'd revisit - and two of these are privacy, not performance
privacy leaks at the SUBSCRIPTION boundary, not the display boundary
a server subscribes to a friend's channel and THEN filters by distance, so it receives that friend's exact position even
when they are 500 miles away and should be invisible. Nothing reaches the user, but the data crossed a process boundary it
did not need to. Geohash-prefixed channels would fix this structurally - a stronger argument than the efficiency case.
1.15 TB/day of precise location history has no stated purpose beyond 'analytics and ML'
that is a lot of permanently-retained location data collected without a specific use - a privacy liability as much as a cost
one. A defensible design would down-sample hard (one point per 5 minutes instead of per 30 seconds cuts it 10x) and set a
retention limit derived from an actual use case.
no GDPR erasure path
a deletion request must remove rows from Cassandra (spread across bucket partitions), the Kafka backlog, the object-storage
archive and any warehouse copy. Cassandra deletes are TOMBSTONES that reclaim no space until compaction, so 'deleted' and
'gone' differ by a compaction cycle. None of this is modelled.
bidirectional friendship storage has no consistency verifier
both rows must be written together, and a partial write leaves an ASYMMETRIC friendship where A sees B but not vice versa -
which shows up as a confusing one-way visibility bug rather than an error. A periodic symmetry check belongs here.
